stem_html:
Historian Priya Raghunathan cautions that the ledgers of the Dutch East India Company are ______ documents. The clerks entered only what the directors in Amsterdam had asked to be told, so the silences in the columns are as deliberate as the entries.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "partial"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "meticulous", "trap": "vocab-collocation"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "fraudulent", "trap": "too-extreme"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "inscrutable", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The word that lives next to the noun. “Meticulous records” is a fixed pairing, and the eye reaches for it before the second sentence is read.
  • Escalating the charge. Leaving material out on instruction is not fraud; one of the choices upgrades an omission into a lie.
  • Answering from the first sentence. Every piece of evidence for the blank sits in the sentence after it.

Why A is right Partial carries both senses the second sentence needs: incomplete, and shaped by an interest. The clerks entered only what was asked for, and the silences in the columns are as deliberate as the entries — a record that is missing things on purpose.

Why B is wrong Meticulous is the word that attaches itself to ledgers by habit, and the sentence gives no evidence about care or accuracy. A meticulous ledger and a partial one are not alternatives; the clerks could be both.

Why C is wrong Fraudulent claims the clerks entered falsehoods. Raghunathan says only that they left things out on instruction, which is a much weaker charge, and the passage never questions the truth of what was written down.

Why D is wrong Inscrutable says the ledgers cannot be read or understood. Raghunathan is reading them, and drawing conclusions from what is absent, so they are legible — they are just not complete.

stem_html:
In her account of the beavers reintroduced to the Scottish Highlands, Ferreira is careful not to ______ the animals' effect. The new dams did raise the water table across two hectares, but the salmon counts she cites move within the range the river showed before any beaver arrived.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "overstate"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "understate", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "measure", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "sensationalize", "trap": "too-extreme"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Flipping the polarity. “Careful not to” already contains one negation; a second one in the choice is easy to lose track of.
  • Grabbing the strongest word. The most dramatic choice is not the most precise one, and the evidence only supports a mild version of the claim.
  • Stopping at the concession. “The new dams did raise the water table” is the half of the sentence that agrees; the half after “but” is the half that decides.

Why A is right The second sentence concedes one real effect and then withholds a second: the salmon counts move within the range the river showed before any beaver arrived. That is a writer keeping a claim small, so what she avoids is overstating.

Why B is wrong Understate reverses the sentence. If Ferreira were avoiding understatement she would be arguing the beavers did more than they appear to, and the salmon evidence she supplies cuts the other way.

Why C is wrong Measure is something Ferreira plainly does — she gives two hectares and a count. A writer is not careful to avoid measuring, and the contrast the sentence sets up is about size of claim, not about whether numbers appear.

Why D is wrong Sensationalize is overstatement plus an accusation of bad faith. Nothing here suggests Ferreira is resisting a temptation to be lurid; she is resisting a temptation to credit the beavers with the salmon.

stem_html:
Choreographer Yun Ha-eun's notation system is ______ rather than prescriptive. A page records where a dancer's weight fell during a performance that has already happened, and two dancers reading the same page will not produce the same phrase.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "descriptive"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "improvisational", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "imprecise", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "authoritative", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Ignoring “rather than.” The blank is defined by opposition; one choice is simply a synonym for the term it is opposed to.
  • The true-but-wrong-target trap. A choice can be an accurate remark about the dancers and still say nothing about the notation.
  • Confusing effect with definition. Two dancers differing is a consequence of the system, not a name for it.

Why A is right The blank is set against “prescriptive,” so it must name the opposite of telling a dancer what to do. A page records where a dancer's weight fell during a performance that has already happened — a report of the past, which is what descriptive means.

Why B is wrong Improvisational describes how a dance is made, not what a notation does. The notation itself is written after the fact and is fixed on the page; it is the reading of it that varies.

Why C is wrong Imprecise is true of the outcome and wrong about the cause. The page may be exact about where the weight fell; what it does not do is issue instructions, and that is the distinction the sentence draws.

Why D is wrong Authoritative is a synonym for the word the sentence is contrasting the blank with. A notation that carried authority would be prescriptive, so this choice puts the sentence at war with itself.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2021 article on urban soil.

Soil scientists have long assumed that the lead in a city garden travels upward from below, and so have advised gardeners to raise beds above the contaminated layer. Tracking lead isotopes in eleven Chicago plots, Okonjo found that the lead in the top four centimetres matched the signature of exterior paint, not of the subsoil — it had blown in and settled from the buildings alongside. The raised beds in her sample were as heavily contaminated as the ground beds. Okonjo notes that her plots were all within twelve metres of a pre-1960 structure.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "It presents a finding that undercuts the reasoning behind a standard recommendation, then notes a limit on that finding."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "It explains why lead accumulates in urban soil and recommends a method for removing it.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "It shows that raised beds are unsafe and calls for the practice to be abandoned.", "trap": "too-extreme"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "It describes a technique for tracking lead isotopes and reports the number of plots the technique was used on.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Promoting a detail to the thesis. The isotope method and the plot count are the most technical things in the passage, which makes them feel important.
  • Finishing the author's argument for her. A finding that undermines advice is not the same as a call to stop following it.
  • Skipping the last sentence. The sentence about twelve metres is what makes the answer say “then notes a limit.”

Why A is right The text opens with the standard advice to raise beds, reports a result that removes its rationale — the lead had blown in and settled from the buildings alongside — and closes on a restriction: her plots were all within twelve metres of a pre-1960 structure. Finding plus limit is exactly the shape.

Why B is wrong No removal method appears anywhere in the text. Okonjo diagnoses where the lead comes from; she never says what to do about it, and a purpose statement cannot add a recommendation the passage withholds.

Why C is wrong The text says the raised beds in her sample were as contaminated as the ground beds, which is a result in eleven plots, not a verdict on the practice. The final sentence exists precisely to stop that leap.

Why D is wrong Isotope tracking and the count of plots are real details, but they are the means, not the point. A purpose built out of the method leaves out both the advice being challenged and the challenge itself.

stem_html:
The following text is from Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 1898 book Women and Economics.

We are the only animal species in which the female depends on the male for food, the only animal species in which the sex-relation is also an economic relation. With us an entire sex lives in a relation of bondage to the other. It is not that women are weaker; the ant and the bee, far smaller, provide for themselves and for the state besides.

Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "It offers a counterexample that rules out a possible explanation for the condition the text has described."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "It provides evidence that insects are better organized than human societies are.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "It concedes that the claim made earlier in the text applies only to certain species.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "It illustrates the economic relation the text introduces in its first sentence.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Reading a semicolon as an example marker. What follows a semicolon often illustrates; here it refutes.
  • Answering the sentence, not the function. Three choices are things the clause mentions; only one is what the clause does for the argument.
  • Missing the negation before it. “It is not that women are weaker” is the claim the underlined portion supports, and it is a denial.

Why A is right The sentence before the underlined portion raises and rejects an explanation: it is not that women are weaker. The insects are brought in to close that door — the ant and the bee, far smaller, provide for themselves, so smallness cannot be the cause.

Why B is wrong Organization is not the comparison being made. Gilman cites the insects for their size relative to their self-sufficiency, and any claim about how well insect societies are run is imported from outside the text.

Why C is wrong It concedes nothing. The underlined clause is doing the opposite of narrowing Gilman's claim; it removes the one excuse a reader might have offered for the human arrangement.

Why D is wrong The economic relation is the human one, in which the female depends on the male for food. The insects are contrasted with that relation, not an instance of it.

stem_html:
Text 1

The sudden spread of a technique across unrelated workshops is the clearest evidence archaeologists have of contact between them. When potters four hundred kilometres apart begin, within a generation, to temper clay with crushed shell, someone carried the idea across that distance.

Text 2

Adeyemi grants that shell tempering appears almost simultaneously at both sites. She notes, however, that both regions saw the same shift to a wetter climate in those decades, and that shell temper is the one local material that keeps a vessel from cracking as humidity swings. Potters who never met would have been pushed toward the same solution by the same problem.

Based on the texts, how would Adeyemi (Text 2) most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "By arguing that a shared constraint can produce the same technique independently, so simultaneity alone does not establish contact."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "By denying that the two groups of potters adopted shell tempering at anything like the same time.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "By agreeing that contact occurred but disputing the direction in which the technique travelled.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "By pointing out that shell temper is a poor material and that its spread therefore requires a social explanation.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Assuming disagreement means denying the fact. Adeyemi grants Text 1's observation and rejects only what Text 1 concludes from it.
  • Disputing the wrong link. One choice argues about where the technique came from, a question Text 2 never reaches.
  • Inverting the evidence. The usefulness of shell temper is the load-bearing detail; a choice that calls it poor has read it backwards.

Why A is right Adeyemi accepts the timing and attacks the inference. Both regions saw the same shift to a wetter climate, and shell temper is the one local material that keeps a vessel from cracking, so the same problem could produce the same answer twice without anyone travelling.

Why B is wrong She concedes the timing in her first sentence: shell tempering appears almost simultaneously at both sites. Denying it would throw away the fact she is explaining.

Why C is wrong Direction of travel never comes up in Text 2. Adeyemi is questioning whether anything travelled at all, which is a disagreement one step earlier than the one this choice describes.

Why D is wrong Text 2 says the opposite — shell temper is the material that works, which is precisely why two independent groups would land on it. Calling it poor removes the mechanism her argument runs on.

stem_html:
Ecologist Tomas Bergstrom hypothesized that the barn swallows nesting inside a livestock shed are quicker to abandon a nest when disturbed than the swallows nesting on its outside wall, because the interior birds have more alternative sites available within the same structure.

Which finding, if true, would most directly support Bergstrom's hypothesis?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Interior nests were abandoned after fewer disturbances than exterior nests were, and the sheds with the most unused interior ledges showed the largest gap."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Interior nests were abandoned after fewer disturbances than exterior nests were, and interior nests held fewer eggs on average.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Swallows nesting inside a shed returned to the same shed in a greater proportion of following years than swallows nesting on the outside wall did.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Sheds with more unused interior ledges were disturbed by farm workers more often than sheds with fewer such ledges.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Matching only the outcome. Two choices report that interior nests are abandoned sooner; only one also ties that to the stated cause.
  • The rival explanation smuggled in as extra support. A second fact that would explain the result by itself is not support, it is competition.
  • A different behaviour that sounds like the same one. Returning next year and staying put today are separate measurements.

Why A is right The hypothesis has two parts and this choice supplies both. The interior birds abandon sooner, and the effect grows with the supply of alternatives — the interior birds have more alternative sites available, which is the reason Bergstrom gives.

Why B is wrong The first half matches and the second half supplies a rival explanation. A bird with less invested in a clutch may leave sooner for that reason alone, so this finding weakens the proposed mechanism as much as it supports the pattern.

Why C is wrong Returning in later years is site fidelity across seasons, not abandonment under disturbance within one. A bird can come back every spring and still leave readily when a person walks in.

Why D is wrong This links ledges to disturbance rather than ledges to abandonment. If anything it introduces a confound: the interior birds would be leaving more because they are bothered more, which is not what Bergstrom claims.

stem_html:
In a 2023 paper, materials scientist Ingrid Wahl reported that a cellulose film she developed stays clear after prolonged exposure to ultraviolet light, unlike conventional plant-based films, which yellow. Wahl claims the film's resistance comes from lignin residues left in the pulp rather than from the coating applied afterward.

Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Wahl's claim?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Uncoated films made from the same pulp stayed clear under ultraviolet light, while coated films made from lignin-free pulp yellowed."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Coated films made from the same pulp stayed clear under ultraviolet light for longer than any conventional plant-based film did.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "The coating Wahl applied is chemically identical to the coating used on conventional plant-based films.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Films made from lignin-free pulp were thinner and tore more easily than films made from Wahl's pulp.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Confirming the result instead of the cause. The claim is causal, so restating that the film works is not support.
  • Failing to vary one thing at a time. Only one choice breaks the two candidate causes apart.
  • A near-miss that argues by elimination. Ruling the coating out is not the same as ruling lignin in.

Why A is right Wahl's claim is about which of two things is doing the work, so the evidence has to separate them. The film that stays clear after prolonged exposure to ultraviolet light keeps its clarity without the coating and loses it without the lignin. Removing the coating and keeping the lignin preserves the effect; removing the lignin and keeping the coating destroys it. That is the comparison her claim needs.

Why B is wrong This shows the film performs, which nobody disputes, and it holds both candidate causes in place at once. A film that is coated and lignin-rich cannot tell you which of the two kept it clear.

Why C is wrong An identical coating makes the coating a less likely explanation, which points in the right direction, but it says nothing about lignin and leaves open that some third feature of Wahl's pulp is responsible.

Why D is wrong Tear strength is a different property. A film can be tougher and still yellow, so this finding cannot bear on the film's resistance to ultraviolet light.

stem_html:
A team compared how long four groups of volunteers could hold a plank position after each group listened to a different type of audio. The team concluded that the effect of the audio depended on whether it had a steady beat rather than on whether volunteers said they enjoyed it.

Volunteers rated dance music and ambient music as equally enjoyable and rated the metronome as the least enjoyable of the three audio types.

Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the team's conclusion?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "The metronome and dance music groups both held the plank about 25 seconds longer than the ambient music group did."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "The metronome group held the plank longer than the dance music group did.", "trap": "axis-misread"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "The ambient music group held the plank longer than the silence group did.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "The dance music group held the plank longer than the silence group did.", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Reading a 2-second gap as a result. The two tallest bars are within noise of each other, and the conclusion never separates them.
  • Picking a true reading that proves nothing. A comparison between two no-beat conditions cannot show that beat is what matters.
  • Ignoring the enjoyment ratings. The sentence under the graph is what makes one comparison decisive and another one useless.

Why A is right The team concluded that the effect of the audio depended on whether it had a steady beat rather than on whether volunteers said they enjoyed it. The two groups with a beat, at 96 and 94 seconds, are close to each other and roughly 25 seconds above ambient at 71 — even though the metronome was rated least enjoyable and dance music was rated as enjoyable as ambient. That is the pattern the conclusion describes.

Why B is wrong The 2-second difference between 96 and 94 is the smallest gap on the chart, and the conclusion does not rank the two beat conditions against each other. Reading it as meaningful is reading the axis more finely than it can be read.

Why C is wrong The 3-second gap between 71 and 68 involves neither of the beat conditions, so it cannot show that a beat is what matters. It is a true reading of the graph that is silent on the claim.

Why D is wrong Dance music beating silence is consistent with the conclusion but does not test it, because dance music was also the more enjoyable of the two. Only a comparison that holds enjoyment apart from beat can support the team.

stem_html: In The Custom of the Country (1913), Edith Wharton presents Undine Spragg as a character whose desires are formed entirely by what she sees other people wanting, so that no wish of hers survives its own satisfaction. Which quotation from a fictional novel would best illustrate this claim?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "“The box she had coveted all winter was hers at last, and from it she watched the boxes above her, where the season's real people sat.”"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "“She had wanted the box all winter, and when it was hers she sat in it every night until the season closed.”", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "“She never wanted anything that was not costly, and the price of a thing was the first question she asked of it.”", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "“She had learned early that a wish spoken aloud in that house was a wish denied, and so she kept her own counsel.”", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Illustrating half the claim. The claim has two moving parts — desires copied from others, and desires that die on being met — and two choices supply exactly one each.
  • The quotation that contradicts on the second beat. Reading only the first clause of B makes it look right.
  • Mistaking a character trait for the mechanism. Loving expensive things is a description; it is not the process the claim names.

Why A is right Both halves of the claim appear: the desire is copied, and no wish of hers survives its own satisfaction. The wish is borrowed — the box was coveted because others had it — and it dies on arrival, because the moment it is hers she is looking upward at the boxes above her, where the season's real people sat.

Why B is wrong Sitting in the box every night is a wish that survives being satisfied, which is the reverse of what Wharton is said to present. The borrowed origin is there; the collapse is not.

Why C is wrong Costliness is a rule about what she wants, and it is stable rather than socially copied. It also shows nothing about what happens once she has the thing, which is half of the claim.

Why D is wrong This is about concealing a wish from a family, not about where the wish came from or what becomes of it. Strategy in a household is a different subject altogether.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2020 article about salt marshes.

A salt marsh keeps pace with a rising sea by trapping sediment among its stems and building its own surface upward. Whether it can keep pace is usually treated as a question about the rate of rise. Delacroix's survey of thirty marshes on the Louisiana coast suggests it is more nearly a question about supply: the marshes that fell behind were not those facing the fastest rise but those downstream of the dammed rivers, where the sediment that used to arrive each spring no longer does. Where sediment remained plentiful, marshes matched even the steepest rates in her sample.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "What limits a marsh's ability to keep pace with a rising sea is more often the sediment available to it than the speed of the rise."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Marshes downstream of dammed rivers are disappearing faster than any other coastal habitat in Louisiana.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Salt marshes build their surfaces upward by trapping sediment among their stems.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "The rate at which the sea is rising has little effect on whether a salt marsh survives.", "trap": "too-extreme"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Taking the setup sentence as the thesis. The first sentence explains the mechanism so the finding can land; it is not the finding.
  • Hardening a comparison into a dismissal. “More nearly a question about supply” ranks two causes; it does not delete one.
  • Inventing the comparison class. One choice ranks marshes against habitats the passage never mentions.

Why A is right The passage names the usual framing, then replaces it: the marshes that fell behind were not those facing the fastest rise but those downstream of the dammed rivers. Supply beats rate as the limiting factor, which is the whole argument.

Why B is wrong No other coastal habitat is mentioned, and no rate of disappearance is given. The comparison this choice makes lies entirely outside the text.

Why C is wrong This is the first sentence, offered as background so the rest can be understood. It is true and it is not the point; the point is what happens when the sediment stops arriving.

Why D is wrong Delacroix does not dismiss the rate of rise. Her marshes matched even the steepest rates when sediment was plentiful, which makes rate a factor that supply can overcome, not a factor with little effect.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2019 profile of the composer Julius Eastman.

Eastman's scores give pitches and durations but almost never give instrumentation, and the four surviving recordings of Stay On It use four different ensembles. Critics have taken this as evidence that Eastman was indifferent to timbre. The letters Ntuli has recovered show something else: Eastman chose the players for each performance himself, sometimes travelling to hear a musician before inviting them. What the score omits, he settled in the room.

According to the text, what is true about Eastman's approach to instrumentation?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "He made instrumentation decisions in person for each performance instead of fixing them in the score."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "He was indifferent to timbre, as the variety of the surviving recordings shows.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "He specified instrumentation in his letters rather than in his scores.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "He preferred that each ensemble performing his work choose its own instrumentation.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Answering with the view being refuted. The critics' reading is stated plainly and then overturned two sentences later.
  • Confusing the evidence with the practice. The letters document the decision; they are not where it was recorded.
  • Assuming an unspecified score means an open one. Silence on paper is not the same as freedom for the performers.

Why A is right The last two sentences say it directly: Eastman chose the players for each performance himself, and what the score omits, he settled in the room. The decision was made, just not on paper.

Why B is wrong This is the reading the passage introduces in order to correct. The critics are quoted, and then Ntuli's letters show something else, so attributing it to the text is quoting the side that loses.

Why C is wrong The letters are Ntuli's evidence about what Eastman did, not the place where Eastman wrote his instrumentation down. The passage says he settled it in the room, in person.

Why D is wrong Ensembles choosing for themselves is the opposite of a composer travelling to hear a musician before inviting them. The variety across recordings came from his choices, not from theirs.

stem_html:
Lichens grow at rates so consistent that the diameter of a colony can date the rock surface beneath it. The method assumes a colony begins growing soon after the surface is exposed. On the moraines of one Norwegian glacier, however, the largest colonies on surfaces of known age are consistently smaller than the method predicts, and the shortfall is greatest on the surfaces that were exposed earliest. Since the growth rate has been measured directly at this site and matches the standard figure, it follows that ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "colonization of a newly exposed surface at this site took longer the earlier the surface was exposed."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "the growth rate of lichens at this site is slower than the standard figure suggests.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "the surfaces on these moraines were exposed more recently than their known ages indicate.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "lichen dating cannot be applied to glacial moraines anywhere.", "trap": "too-extreme"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Attacking a premise instead of drawing the conclusion. The rate is stated to be verified; a choice that denies it is not an inference.
  • Overlooking the second data point. The conclusion has to explain not just the shortfall but why it grows with the age of the surface.
  • Generalising past the evidence. One site does not license a claim about moraines anywhere.

Why A is right Age and rate are both fixed here, so the only free term is the delay before growth starts. A colony that is too small on a surface of known age has had less growing time than the surface has had years, and the shortfall is greatest on the surfaces that were exposed earliest, so the delay was longest there.

Why B is wrong The passage forecloses this: the growth rate has been measured directly at this site and matches the standard figure. Choosing it means contradicting a premise the sentence supplies specifically to rule it out.

Why C is wrong The ages are given as known, and the surfaces would have to be younger by different amounts in a pattern that tracks their age — a coincidence the text gives no reason to accept when a single explanation is available.

Why D is wrong One glacier's moraines cannot settle what happens everywhere, and the passage is explaining a local discrepancy rather than retiring the method.

stem_html:
Shoppers presented with two versions of a product often choose the cheaper one; presented with three, they often choose the middle one, even when the middle option is the same product at the same price as the earlier cheaper one. Researchers testing this effect on a menu found the pattern held for wine but disappeared for desserts, and noted that their diners reported far more confidence in judging a dessert than in judging a wine. This suggests that the pull toward the middle option depends on ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "how uncertain a shopper is about judging the product's quality on its own."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "how many options a shopper is presented with at once.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "the difference in price between the cheapest and the most expensive option.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "whether the product is one the shopper will consume immediately.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Naming the setup as the cause. Three options is what makes the effect possible in both conditions, so it cannot be what separates them.
  • Reaching for the intuitive economic variable. Price spread is never measured here.
  • Skipping the clause after “and noted.” The confidence finding is the only difference the passage reports, so it is the only one available.

Why A is right Wine and dessert differ in the one respect the passage reports: diners reported far more confidence in judging a dessert than in judging a wine. The effect appears where confidence is low and vanishes where it is high, so uncertainty is what it tracks.

Why B is wrong Three options were on offer in both cases, so the number cannot explain why the effect appeared in one and not the other. It is a condition for the effect, not the variable the last sentence is asking about.

Why C is wrong No prices are given for either the wine or the desserts, and the passage never compares spreads. This is a plausible influence that the text supplies no evidence about.

Why D is wrong Both a wine and a dessert are consumed at the meal, so this does not distinguish the two cases even though it is a real difference between restaurant and retail settings.

stem_html:
The archaeologist Ines Cardoso spent nine seasons excavating a single Iron Age roundhouse in Devon ______ sequence of floors she recorded there is now the reference against which other British roundhouses are dated.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "; the"}, {"letter": "B", "content": ", the", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "the", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "D", "content": ": the", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The length of the first clause. Nine seasons, a single roundhouse and a county make the opening feel like a long introductory phrase rather than a complete sentence.
  • The colon that almost fits. A colon is defensible whenever the second part feels like a payoff, which is why it is the tempting wrong answer.
  • Checking only the second clause. Both sides have to be independent before a semicolon is right, and the test is to read each half alone.

Why A is right Two independent clauses meet here — Cardoso spent nine seasons, and the sequence is now the reference — with no conjunction between them. A semicolon is the punctuation that joins two independent clauses on its own.

Why B is wrong A comma alone between two independent clauses is a splice. The second clause has its own subject and verb and could stand as a sentence, so a comma is not strong enough.

Why C is wrong Running the two clauses together with no punctuation at all is a fused sentence, which is the same error as the comma splice without the comma.

Why D is wrong A colon promises that what follows explains or specifies what came before. The second clause here reports a consequence of the work rather than spelling out what the work was, so the colon oversells the link.

stem_html:
Because the telescope's mirror is segmented ______ of its eighteen hexagons has to be aligned to within a fraction of a wavelength of the others.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": ", each"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "; each", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "each", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": ": each", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two clauses, so a semicolon. The count of clauses is not the test; whether each can stand alone is.
  • The subordinator hiding at the very start. One word at the front of the sentence decides every other mark in it.
  • A colon for a cause-and-effect feel. A colon needs a complete sentence to its left, whatever the logical relationship is.

Why A is right “Because” makes the first clause subordinate, so it is an introductory element attached to the main clause that follows. A comma is the punctuation that separates a leading subordinate clause from its main clause.

Why B is wrong A semicolon joins two independent clauses. The first clause here opens with “Because” and cannot stand alone, so a semicolon has nothing to join on its left.

Why C is wrong No punctuation is not wrong in the way a splice is, but a subordinate clause of this length placed in front of its main clause takes a comma in Standard English.

Why D is wrong A colon must follow an independent clause. “Because the telescope's mirror is segmented” is a fragment, so a colon cannot stand there no matter how well the second half explains the first.

stem_html:
The composer's best-known work, a setting of a fourteenth-century Welsh poem ______ written in three weeks and has never been out of print since.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": ", was"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "was", "trap": "modifier-attachment"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "; was", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": ": was", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The unpaired comma. A nonessential element takes a mark at both ends, and the missing one is the second.
  • Reading “poem” as the subject. The verb belongs to “work,” five words earlier.
  • Any stronger mark here splits subject from verb, which no punctuation in Standard English is allowed to do.

Why A is right “A setting of a fourteenth-century Welsh poem” is a nonessential appositive renaming the subject. It opened with a comma, so it has to close with one before the verb picks the sentence back up.

Why B is wrong Leaving the second comma out strands the appositive: the reader gets a comma that opens an interruption and no mark that ends it, so the subject appears to run straight into the verb through the middle of a phrase.

Why C is wrong A semicolon would break the subject away from its own verb. “Was written in three weeks” has no subject of its own, so nothing on the right of the semicolon can stand alone.

Why D is wrong A colon also demands an independent clause on each side of the relationship it sets up, and here it would cut the sentence between its subject and its verb.

stem_html:
Marine biologist Ayana Elizabeth Johnson has argued that the most useful thing a coastal town can protect is not its reef but its ______ mangroves absorb storm surge, hold sediment in place, and shelter the juveniles of the very fish the reef is prized for.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "mangroves: "}, {"letter": "B", "content": "mangroves, ", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "mangroves ", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "mangroves and ", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The word before the blank is also the subject after it. “Mangroves” can end the first clause or begin the second, and only one reading survives the rest of the sentence.
  • Three items in a list after the break make the second half feel subordinate when it is in fact a full clause.
  • The coordinating conjunction that drops its comma. Adding “and” without a comma is an error even where the logic would allow it.

Why A is right The first clause is complete at “mangroves,” and everything after spells out why mangroves are the answer. A colon after an independent clause is exactly the mark for an elaboration of that kind.

Why B is wrong The material after the break is an independent clause with its own subject and three verbs, so a comma alone between it and the clause before is a splice.

Why C is wrong With no punctuation the sentence fuses, and it also becomes momentarily unreadable: “its mangroves absorb storm surge” parses as a single clause until the reader hits the second verb.

Why D is wrong “And” would coordinate the two clauses as equals, but it needs a comma before it, and it loses the relationship the sentence is built on — the second clause justifies the first rather than adding to it.

stem_html:
The set of instructions that governs how a cell's proteins are folded, along with the enzymes that read them, ______ still only partly understood.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "is"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "are", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "have been", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "were", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Twenty words between subject and verb. The nearest noun before the blank is plural and is not the subject.
  • “Along with” is not “and.” It adds information about the subject without adding to it.
  • “Still” fixes the tense. Two of the choices change the tense as well as the number, which is easy to miss while checking agreement.

Why A is right The subject is “the set,” which is singular. Everything between it and the verb — a relative clause and an “along with” phrase — is modification, and “along with” does not make a compound subject the way “and” would.

Why B is wrong Plural agreement takes its cue from “proteins,” “enzymes” or the “along with” phrase, none of which is the subject. Strip the modifiers and the sentence is “the set is.”

Why C is wrong This is plural for the same wrong reason and also shifts the tense into the present perfect, which the sentence gives no occasion for.

Why D is wrong Past tense contradicts “still,” which places the state of understanding in the present, and it is plural besides.

Having spent four years cataloguing the flute repertoire of the Andean highlands, ______

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

Traps in this question

  • The right person appears in every choice. Three of them mention Quispe; only one makes Quispe the grammatical subject.
  • Meaning that survives the error. All four sentences are easy to understand, so ear alone will not sort them.
  • The expletive “it.” A subject with no content cannot be the one who spent four years doing anything.

Why A is right An opening participial phrase attaches to the subject of the main clause, so whoever spent four years cataloguing has to be named there. Quispe is the subject, and Quispe did the cataloguing.

Why B is wrong This makes “the piece” the subject, which says the piece spent four years cataloguing the repertoire. The sentence is comprehensible and still ungrammatical for exactly that reason.

Why C is wrong The subject is the gerund phrase “identifying the piece,” so the act of identifying is what did the cataloguing. Naming Quispe later in the clause does not repair the attachment.

Why D is wrong “It” is an expletive subject with no referent at all, which leaves the participial phrase modifying nothing.

By the time the survey team reached the summit cairn, the storm that had delayed them for two days ______ south, and the ridge below was clear for the first time that week.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "had moved"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "has moved", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "moves", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "moving", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A past perfect already in the sentence. “Had delayed” belongs to the relative clause, and it is tempting to treat it as the one the sentence needed.
  • “By the time” is the sequence marker, and it requires the earlier event to be marked as earlier.
  • The participle that reads smoothly aloud. Fluency is not finiteness.

Why A is right Two past events are ordered here: the team reached the cairn, and before that the storm left. The past perfect is what marks the earlier of two past events, and “by the time” sets the sequence up.

Why B is wrong The present perfect ties a past event to the present moment, but the whole sentence is anchored in the past by “reached” and “was clear.”

Why C is wrong Simple present puts the storm's movement in the same time as the reader rather than before the team's arrival, and it clashes with every other verb in the sentence.

Why D is wrong A participle is not a finite verb, so this leaves the clause without a predicate and turns the sentence into a fragment joined to a clause.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "the younger curator's"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "her", "trap": "pronoun-ambiguity"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "their", "trap": "pronoun-ambiguity"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "hers", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A pronoun that is grammatical and still wrong. Number and case are fine; the referent is the problem.
  • “Their” as a neutral escape. Here it reunites two people the sentence has just set against each other.
  • Possessive determiner against possessive pronoun. One of these forms cannot precede a noun at all.

Why A is right Two curators are in play and the sentence has to say which one won. Only the noun phrase identifies a person; every pronoun here could point at either of them.

Why B is wrong “Her” has two possible antecedents and the sentence supplies nothing to choose between them, so the reader cannot tell whose argument prevailed.

Why C is wrong “Their” refers to both curators at once, which contradicts the first clause: they disagreed, so a single argument cannot belong to both.

Why D is wrong “Hers” is the independent possessive and cannot sit in front of a noun. “Hers argument” is not a possible English phrase.

stem_html:
Ravens are among the few birds that will hide food while a rival watches and then return, once alone, to move it. Some researchers read this as evidence that a raven models what the rival knows. ______ the behaviour also appears in ravens that have merely been exposed to the sound of a rival, with no bird in sight, which a simpler rule about noise and risk would explain just as well.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Yet"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Therefore", "trap": "transition-reversal"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Likewise", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "For instance", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The example that is really a counterexample. The third sentence looks like more of the same behaviour, and it is offered against the interpretation.
  • “Simpler rule” is the tell. Offering a cheaper explanation is an act of opposition.
  • Reading only up to the comma. The clause after “which” is where the sentence declares its side.

Why A is right The third sentence undercuts the second: if the sound alone is enough, the richer explanation is no longer required. A contrastive transition is what marks a sentence that weakens the claim before it.

Why B is wrong “Therefore” makes the third sentence follow from the second, but the evidence about sound is a reason to doubt the mind-reading account, not a consequence of it.

Why C is wrong “Likewise” announces a parallel case pointing the same way. The two sentences point opposite ways, so the parallel is exactly what is missing.

Why D is wrong An example of a raven modelling a rival's knowledge would have to involve a rival being modelled. Here there is no bird in sight, which is what makes the sentence a counterexample rather than an instance.

stem_html:
Tidal power is unusually predictable: the times and heights of the tides can be computed decades ahead, so a grid operator knows exactly when the turbines will deliver. That reliability comes at a cost. ______ a tidal barrage can only be built where the range between high and low water is large, and there are fewer than forty such sites worldwide.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Specifically,"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Nevertheless,", "trap": "transition-reversal"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "In contrast,", "trap": "transition-reversal"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Consequently,", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “That reliability comes at a cost” is a promise, and the next sentence pays it. Elaboration, not contrast.
  • The word “cost” invites a concession. Two choices reverse the direction for that reason alone.
  • Consequence against composition. The site limit is what the cost is, not something the cost produced.

Why A is right The sentence before announces a cost without naming it, and the sentence after names it. A transition that promises detail is what carries a general statement into its particulars.

Why B is wrong “Nevertheless” would set the site limitation against the cost, but the limitation is the cost. There is nothing here for it to push back on.

Why C is wrong “In contrast” needs two things being compared. The two sentences describe one thing at two levels of detail.

Why D is wrong “Consequently” would make the shortage of sites a result of the cost just mentioned. The geography of tidal ranges is not caused by anything in the passage; it is what the cost consists of.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Sourdough starters are cultures of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria.
  • Bakers often claim a starter takes on the character of the city it is kept in.
  • Reese sampled 40 starters from 4 continents and sequenced their microbes.
  • Starters from the same city were no more similar to one another than to starters from other cities.
  • Starters fed the same flour were markedly similar to one another regardless of location.

The student wants to present the study's finding to an audience already familiar with sourdough. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

Traps in this question

  • Presenting the setup instead of the result. Two choices stop at method or definition.
  • The half-finding. Reporting only that city did not matter loses the explanation that replaces it.
  • Ignoring the stated audience. Familiar readers make the definition note the one to leave out.

Why A is right The finding has two halves — city does not predict, flour does — and only this choice states both, with the scale of the study attached. It also skips the definition, which an audience already familiar with sourdough does not need.

Why B is wrong This is definition plus method and no result. The audience is stipulated to know what a starter is, so the one sentence spent explaining it is the one sentence wasted.

Why C is wrong The bakers' claim and the method are here; what Reese found is not. A reader reaches the end without learning whether the claim survived.

Why D is wrong This gives the negative half of the finding alone. Without the flour result the study reads as an absence of any pattern, which is not what Reese reported.
